title: When the stars retreat
hookLine: glorify Him when you rise and at the retreat of the stars (52:48–49)

lines: THE VERY END OF THE NIGHT.
THE STARS GO OUT, ONE BY ONE.
cards: At the very end of the night, the sky is still dark, but something has already shifted. The faint stars go first. Then the brighter ones, one by one, as if someone were walking through a house turning off lamps.
Birds start before there's any light to speak of, and the whole change is over quickly. Surah At-Tur ends exactly there, at that hour, and tells the Prophet ﷺ what to do with it.

teach.b: The last two verses of At-Tur begin with comfort. Wait patiently for your Lord's decree, they tell the Prophet, for you are in Our sight.

The Arabic is bi-a'yunina, literally within Our eyes: watched over, never out of view. Then the instruction, in Pickthall's translation: "And in the night-time also hymn His praise, and at the setting of the stars."

teach.h: IDBAR AN-NUJUM: THE STARS TURN BACK.
teach.b: Idbar an-nujum: the turning back of the stars, their retreat as dawn comes. Three times for glorifying, tasbih, are named across these two verses: when you rise, in the night, and as the stars withdraw.
Commentators connected idbar an-nujum with the two short units of prayer before the dawn prayer, the sunnah of Fajr. A report attributed to Ibn 'Abbas says so, and other commentators followed him.
The hadith tradition treats those two units with unusual tenderness.

In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says the two units before dawn are better than the world and everything in it. 'A'ishah reported, in Bukhari, that he was never more regular in any voluntary prayer than in those two.
Notice the shape. It doesn't say glorify Him in the bright, busy middle of the day.

teach.h: PRAISE AT THE EDGES OF THE DAY.
teach.b: It says, in effect: at the edges, when you've just risen and the night is letting go, the hours when nobody needs you yet. Subhanallah is the phrase of tasbih: glory be to Allah, far above every flaw.
Said as the stars fade, it meets the day before the day starts asking things of you.

how: Many Muslims pray two short voluntary units before the obligatory dawn prayer, and say subhanallah, often thirty-three times, after prayers and in the early morning.

o: glorifying God: glory be to Allah
asking God to forgive a sin
a prayer said only on Fridays

games.q: you're awake as the last stars fade. what do commentators link idbar an-nujum to?
o: the two units of prayer before dawn.
games.why: a report from Ibn 'Abbas, and commentators after him, tie it to the sunnah of Fajr.

practice: Picture waking before the light, the sky just beginning to thin. With each slow breath, say subhanallah quietly, glory to Allah, counting on your fingers if you like.
If you don't pray, simply hold the picture of the stars going out, one by one, and let your breath slow with them.

wordCard.voice: Tasbih: glorifying God, named three times at the edges of night and day in Surah At-Tur's last verses, as the stars withdraw. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the retreat of the stars (52:49).

carryVoice: Your line: as the stars fade. The first minute can be praise, or simply stillness. That's day five hundred ninety-seven.
